title: CELPIP General Listening — Practice Test 37
instructions: Listen to the audio for each part and answer the questions. Each audio plays once.

listeningScripts.title: Defective Appliance Return
listeningScripts.text: Customer: Hi, I'd like to return a refrigerator I purchased last week. It's still under warranty. Agent: I'd be happy to help with that. Can you tell me what's wrong with it? Customer: Well, the ice maker isn't working, and there's this strange noise coming from the compressor. I've had three fridges before and this one definitely isn't normal. Agent: I understand your concern. How long have you had it? Customer: Six days. I bought it on Tuesday morning from your downtown store. Agent: Okay, and you still have your receipt? Customer: Yes, I have it here. Purchase price was $1,299. Agent: Perfect. Since it's within the seven-day return window, we can definitely process a full refund or exchange for a different model. Do you prefer cash back or would you like to choose another refrigerator? Customer: I'd rather have a refund. Can you process it today? Agent: Absolutely. We'll need to arrange pickup within 48 hours, and the refund will appear in your account within five to seven business days. Would tomorrow morning work for a pickup between 10 and 2 PM?

listeningScripts.title: Workplace Lunch Break
listeningScripts.text: Marcus: Hey, want to grab lunch together? Jessica: Sure, where are you thinking? Marcus: There's that new sushi place across the street. I've heard good things about it. Jessica: I'm not really in the mood for sushi. How about the Thai place on the corner? Marcus: That works too. I haven't tried that one yet. Jessica: They have great pad thai. We should go soon though, it gets busy after noon. Marcus: Good point. How about right now? Jessica: Perfect. I'll grab my wallet. Marcus: Do you think they have vegetarian options? Jessica: Definitely. They have a whole vegetarian section on the menu. Marcus: Great. Shall we? Jessica: Let's go. See you in five minutes downstairs.

listeningScripts.title: University Orientation: First Week Checklist
listeningScripts.text: Hello, welcome to orientation week. I'm here to walk you through essential tasks for your first week. First, attend your faculty's orientation meeting on Monday at ten AM in the Student Centre. Bring your student ID. Second, register for your courses online by Wednesday, August 28th. Early registration means better class times. Third, purchase your textbooks from the university bookstore before classes start. Fourth, get your student photo ID taken at the Services Office between 9 and 4 on any day this week. The photo ID is required for library access and residence entry. Fifth, activate your email account at the IT support desk. Your email is your primary communication channel for all university announcements. Sixth, find your classes on a campus map. Most buildings are located around the central quad. Seventh, attend the Welcome Social on Friday evening in the gymnasium. It's a great way to meet other students and faculty. Eighth, complete your health and immunization form at Student Health Services. This is mandatory before attending classes. Finally, budget about three hundred dollars for books and materials. Questions? Visit the information desk in the main foyer.

listeningScripts.title: Ontario Solar Energy Initiative
listeningScripts.text: Ontario has launched an ambitious solar energy initiative targeting rooftop installations across residential and commercial properties. The program, called SolarON, aims to install solar panels on 50,000 homes and businesses over three years. The government is providing subsidies covering up to 40 percent of installation costs for eligible homeowners. Solar power currently accounts for only 1.2 percent of Ontario's electricity generation, but officials project this could increase to 8 percent by 2030. The initiative includes training programs to develop 2,500 new solar installation technicians. A rebate program offers homeowners up to 8,000 dollars toward equipment and installation expenses. Companies installing solar systems have reported a 150 percent increase in inquiries since the program's announcement. Environmental advocates praise the initiative for reducing carbon emissions and creating green jobs. The average residential system costs approximately 22,000 dollars before subsidies and rebates. Participants are also eligible for net metering, allowing them to sell excess power back to the grid.

listeningScripts.title: University Program Expansion Planning
listeningScripts.text:
Dean Robert: We've been asked to consider expanding our engineering program, particularly in renewable energy studies. The faculty has requested three additional full-time instructors and funding for new laboratory equipment. The cost would be approximately 2.4 million dollars over two years. Given our current budget constraints, I'm hesitant to commit to this expansion.

Professor Elena: I understand the budget concerns, Dean, but we're actually losing enrollment to competing universities who offer these programs. Last year, we lost 150 potential engineering students to schools with stronger renewable energy options. If we don't expand now, we'll fall behind. Plus, there's significant industry demand for graduates with renewable energy expertise. Companies are specifically recruiting from universities with these specialized programs.

Student Representative Malik: From a student perspective, I absolutely support this expansion. Many of my classmates are interested in sustainability and green technology, but we don't have the courses or facilities to support that focus. I think this investment would make our university much more attractive to prospective students, which would actually increase our overall enrollment and revenue.

Budget Committee Member Diana: Malik makes a good point about revenue. If this program attracts even 200 additional students, the tuition revenue would exceed the expansion costs within three years. And we could explore partnerships with industry for funding. I've been in conversations with several renewable energy companies that might contribute equipment or funding in exchange for access to our graduates for recruitment.

listeningScripts.title: Universal Basic Income Feasibility
listeningScripts.text: I want to discuss Universal Basic Income, or UBI, and why I believe it could work in Canada. The concept is straightforward: every citizen receives a regular, unconditional cash payment from the government. Now, I know people immediately worry about the cost, but let me address that. First, UBI could replace many existing welfare programs that are expensive to administer. The bureaucracy involved in means-testing and eligibility verification costs billions. UBI would be simpler and less wasteful. Second, the economic stimulus of putting money in people's hands is significant. When people have financial security, they spend more, which supports businesses and creates jobs. Third, UBI addresses real problems: poverty, economic instability, and lack of opportunity. We've seen pilot projects in Kenya, Finland, and Canada that show positive outcomes. In Kenya, UBI increased business formation by 32 percent. In Finland, participants reported better mental health and less anxiety. Some worry it will make people lazy, but that's not supported by evidence. People want purpose and contribution, not just money. What UBI does is give them the freedom to pursue education, care for family, or start businesses without desperation. The real question isn't whether we can afford UBI—it's whether we can afford not to implement it. Rising inequality and automation are creating unprecedented challenges.
